item.title: Fathers of Daughters Invest Differently
item.description:
Parenting

Fathers of Daughters Invest Differently

Research links pro-woman views and higher performance to parenting girls.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • Fathers of daughters develop measurably stronger support for gender equity across politics, law, and business.
  • VC partners with daughters hire more women, and their funds actually perform better as a result.
  • Rising wealth and smaller families created a tipping point where men backed equity to protect their daughters.

My father was a conservative man, socially and politically, but on one theme he overtook the liberals in their own lane: women’s empowerment. From the time I was old enough to observe, he supported rising and powerful women. Thatcher in the 80s—at least until she started the Falklands War; Madeleine Albright in the 90s; respect for Benazir Bhutto and Corazon Aquino, as well as several business leaders.

A vivid memory I retain is his regularly handing me newspaper articles about powerful women. “Couldn’t you do this?” He was talking about Christine Bortenlänger, who started running the Munich stock exchange at 33, or the then-popular French Prime Minister Édith Cresson. Already in the new millennium, Merkel becoming chancellor was received almost like a confirmation of expectations.

Source: By Rebecca Abell at Dreamstime.com

What explains this progressive view, among many others he held which were rather proudly pre-Renaissance? Being raised by a war widow who had to brave adversity may be one reason. But having a daughter may be another.

Fathers of daughters are pro-woman, in almost everything

Diligent economists have shown that fathers of daughters show greater support for gender equity. US Congressmen vote more pro-woman on relevant issues if they have daughters—and even more so if they have more daughters.

Federal judges with more daughters decide more liberally on women’s issues, and this effect comes, wait for it, mostly from Republican judges. (Dad, you would have been right at home there.)

Parenting daughters is associated with a higher propensity to hire female partners in venture capital firms.

There is a 24% increase in the probability of hiring a senior female investor when a son is replaced with a daughter among existing partners in a firm.

Fathers of daughters invest better

Those senior partners I was talking about, who hire more women because they have daughters, also invest better. The research I mentioned earlier shows that improved gender diversity in the firm—induced by parenting more daughters—improves deal and fund performance. This comes mostly from the daughters of senior partners rather than junior partners (which does not surprise me, because senior partners have more influence).

Let’s think about this for a moment. There is no proof (in this evidence) that an imposed gender quota improves performance. But partners who hire more women because they have daughters find that their teams perform better. Partners whose fundamental worldview is women-friendly, and who act accordingly, perform well. In other words: partners who likely had any possible gender biases radically reduced by having a daughter make better deals.

It makes perfect sense, really. If you are capable of taking an unbiased look at investments and other decisions, you will make better ones—including in hiring.

How we got here: wealth, family planning, and the tipping point

The emergence of women’s empowerment, as well as of men who supported it, has a history. Two-century-long trends have been shown to bring this about.

First, countries became richer and individuals accumulated more capital. Second, family planning became easier. These two depend on a third trend, which is crucial in making family planning possible: spreading education.

How does this mix become a soup? Consider property rights. If they are biased towards husbands versus wives, husbands gain—but only insofar as they don’t have daughters who will lose out in the future to their husbands under the same biased rights. With family planning, there will be more families that only have daughters and no sons. So there will be some men who will suffer greatly seeing their daughters suffer. At the same time, with rising wealth, more and more men will reach a level of economic security that enables them to take risks.

At some level of average wealth and average family size, the scale tips, and men begin to want to change property laws to benefit their daughters more. The scale tips earlier, the more biased the current property rights system. So historically, it tipped earlier in common law countries than in civil law countries.

Source: By Florida Memory on Unsplash

This kind of explanation would have fascinated my history-teaching dad. Sadly, we did not have the chance to discuss it. But if we had, he would have pointed out that while most laws are already changed towards equity, the power balances are not.

Excerpted, in part, from my blog Love-O-Nomics. www.dateconomics.com

item.title: When Targeting One Black Woman, the Message Reaches Millions
item.description:
Race and Ethnicity

When Targeting One Black Woman, the Message Reaches Millions

The emotional fatigue behind repeated exposure to racialized disrespect.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • Public attacks on Black women can trigger emotional responses beyond the target.
  • Many Black women experience chronic social scrutiny affecting daily interactions.
  • Vicarious racism and identity shape emotional reactions to public dehumanization.
  • Repeated exposure to stereotypes can lead to emotional exhaustion and stress.
Source: Dellon Thomas/Pixabay

Public attacks on Black women can trigger emotional responses that extend far beyond the intended target.

At times, it can feel as though Black women are rarely afforded the freedom to simply exist without commentary, criticism, or judgment. When a highly visible Black woman is publicly mocked, degraded, or dehumanized, many Black women experience the incident as more than an insult directed at a single individual. The target may be one woman, but the message often reaches millions.

When I hear derogatory comments about Black women, I feel something that is difficult to explain. The comments are not directed at me personally, yet the emotions are real. My reaction is often immediate and includes frustration, sadness, disappointment, and exhaustion. As a school psychologist, I have wondered why these moments can evoke such strong emotional responses. Why does a comment aimed at someone else feel so personal? Why can an incident involving a public figure linger in our thoughts long after the headlines fade? The answer may lie in the intersection of identity, lived experience, and mental health. Yet, as a Black woman, I already knew the answer.

More Than a Single Comment

For many Black women, these moments are not experienced in isolation. They are layered upon years of subtle and overt messages about who we are and who society believes we should be.

At times, Black women may experience a sense of chronic social scrutiny. Public insults may capture headlines, but they often reflect experiences many Black women encounter in everyday life:

  • Having our competence questioned while others are presumed capable.
  • Seeing our expertise overlooked despite our credentials.
  • Navigating microaggressions that suggest we are less intelligent, less qualified, or less deserving of respect.
  • Feeling pressure to prove ourselves repeatedly in environments where others are given the benefit of the doubt.

As a Black woman with a Ph.D., I have experienced this firsthand. There have been moments when people interacted with me as though I were uninformed or incapable before knowing anything about my education, expertise, or accomplishments. While those moments may seem insignificant in isolation, they accumulate over time. The emotional burden is rarely carried by one interaction. It is carried by years of experiences that communicate the same underlying message. This is why attacks on prominent Black women can feel personal to so many of us. We are not merely reacting to a single event. We are responding to a pattern that feels painfully familiar.

When the Stress Is Vicarious

Researchers have increasingly examined the concept of vicarious racism, which refers to the emotional and psychological impact of witnessing or learning about racism directed toward others. Studies suggest that people can experience distress, anxiety, anger, and emotional fatigue even when they are not the direct target of discrimination. This helps explain why public attacks on prominent Black women can feel personal.

Psychologists Henri Tajfel and John Turner proposed Social Identity Theory, which suggests that individuals derive part of their self-concept from the social groups to which they belong. When someone from our group succeeds, we may experience pride. When someone from our group is ridiculed or dehumanized, we may experience the injury more personally than outsiders expect. This reaction is not necessarily about identifying with a specific individual. It is about recognizing a familiar pattern. For many Black women, the stereotypes embedded within these attacks are not new. They echo messages we have encountered throughout our lives about our intelligence, femininity, appearance, competence, and worth.

Our minds recognize those themes immediately.

The Mental Health Cost of Repeated Exposure

Repeated exposure to negative stereotypes and public attacks can affect mental health in ways that are often overlooked. A single comment may be hurtful. However, many Black women are not responding to a single comment. We are responding to years of accumulated experiences that have taught us to recognize the same narratives in different forms. Researchers studying racial stress have found that repeated exposure to dehumanizing comments and discrimination can create a cumulative psychological burden. Some scholars describe this process as "weathering," the gradual impact that chronic stress can have on emotional well-being and overall health over time.

For Black women, repeated exposure to demeaning messages can contribute to:

  • Emotional exhaustion
  • Hypervigilance
  • Increased stress and anxiety
  • Feelings of sadness and frustration
  • A diminished sense of psychological safety

The burden becomes even heavier when society minimizes or dismisses these experiences. Many Black women are expected to absorb disrespect gracefully and move forward without acknowledging the emotional impact. Yet when we express hurt, frustration, or anger, our reactions are often filtered through stereotypes. Instead of being viewed as normal human responses to mistreatment, they may be labeled as aggression, confrontation, or oversensitivity. The result is a unique form of emotional labor: Managing the experience while simultaneously managing how others perceive our response to it.

Why It Feels So Familiar

People outside the experience often underestimate the impact of these moments. They may see a single comment. Many Black women see a lifetime of similar messages compressed into a single moment. We see reminders of the times our intelligence was questioned, our expertise was dismissed, our accomplishments were minimized, or our humanity was reduced to stereotypes. The target may change, but the underlying message often remains remarkably consistent. That is why the emotional response is not simply outrage. More often, it is exhaustion.

  • Exhaustion from recognizing the pattern
  • Exhaustion from knowing that many young Black girls are listening
  • Exhaustion from understanding that some people will defend the behavior rather than challenge it
  • Exhaustion from realizing how familiar it all feels

Even when I am not the woman being criticized when these comments occur, I feel something.

I suspect many Black women do.

Perhaps the most important question is not why so many Black women react when these incidents occur. Perhaps the better question is why the experience feels so familiar that we recognize it immediately. The answer may be that these moments are never just about one woman. They land in a place many Black women recognize immediately, a place shaped by repeated questions about our belonging, dignity, and humanity. There is anger in that recognition, but also exhaustion. Not because the moment is new, but because it is familiar. So, when a public attack reappears in this form, the emotional impact does not stay with the individual. It moves through memory, through experience, and through a lifetime of being made to feel as though our humanity is still up for debate.

item.title: The Escalation Cycle: Your Roadmap Through a Meltdown
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

The Escalation Cycle: Your Roadmap Through a Meltdown

What every caregiver needs to know about timing, triggers, and big feelings.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • Big feelings follow a predictable arc that caregivers can learn to read before a meltdown peaks.
  • Building relationships and teaching coping skills during calm are powerful meltdown prevention strategies.
  • Prompting a coping strategy works in some phases and backfires in others: Timing is everything.
  • The debrief conversation belongs after full calm returns, not in the aftermath of escalation.

A few weeks ago, someone really ticked me off via email. I could feel the edge in my own typing as I crafted a reply. I was not fine. I was in what researchers call the agitation phase of the escalation cycle, and I didn’t catch it before sending a reply that was harsher than intended. Later, I reflected on the irony of my response, as this exact topic is what my colleague, Dr. Jessica Koslouski, and I have been presenting on with schools all year. I needed my own reminder to quickly draw on a positive coping strategy before responding.

Usually, adults are better at recognizing the escalation cycle because we have lived it repeatedly. Children, however, have had far less practice and live it more visibly as they have yet to establish de-escalation strategies. For caregivers at home and school, understanding the cycle can do more than simply explain the meltdown. It helps guide you on what to do, and what to skip, at each phase in the escalation cycle.

The Cycle: A Quick Map

The cycle of escalation describes a predictable arc from calm to crisis and back. The seven phases are: Calm, Trigger, Agitation, Acceleration, Peak, De-escalation, and Recovery. Each looks different, and as such, calls for a different caregiver response to successfully navigate.

Calm: Where Prevention Lives

The calm phase is when all the proactive work that prevents escalation gets done. When a child is calm, they are most cooperative and responsive, which offers the critical window for learning effective strategies for coping with escalating feelings. Tools for coping in the moment, like Feel Your Best Self, are most effective when children learn and practice them proactively, not during the storm. Think of it like a fire drill: You don't learn the exit plan when the building is on fire.

Three caregiver strategies are well supported by research to help maintain the calm. First, relationship building: Children who feel genuinely supported by multiple adults are more resilient under stress. The practical target is five positive interactions for every one corrective exchange. Second, clear expectations: Children who know what is expected, and what happens when expectations are not met, have something to anchor to when stress rises. Third, providing choice: Perceived loss of control is a common escalation trigger. Giving children meaningful choices in low-stakes moments preserves their sense of agency when pressure increases.

Trigger and Agitation: Catch It Early

A child hits a trigger, like an unexpected change, a perceived rejection, or an unfair correction. They look off-task, restless, withdrawn. Nothing has exploded yet, but something is already happening. That’s the start of the agitation phase.

Consider a 5-year-old who arrives Monday morning quieter than usual, hovering at the edge of the rug instead of joining circle time. His teacher notices and moves close, offering a quiet acknowledgment rather than pressing for participation. That moment of early recognition can change the morning trajectory.

The research framing: Every complaint is an underlying emotion plus an unstated request. The caregiver's job in this phase is to communicate empathy and offer space rather than push forcefully for engagement or questions. This is also a possible window to prompt a coping strategy, if the child already knows one.

Acceleration: The Last Window

Frustration has now become visible behavior, like arguing, refusing, pressing buttons, or shutting down. The child is testing limits and trying to pull others into the conflict. This is still a window for intervention, but the approach must shift to avoid further acceleration.

When a child is in the acceleration phase, caregivers can lend their regulated state by maintaining calm and displaying detachment. Repeated directives and public corrections at this stage can add fuel and should be avoided. Use nonconfrontational limit setting: State the expectation and consequence neutrally, frame it as the child's decision, then walk away and give space. This is the last viable moment to prompt a coping strategy, and it should be kept brief with immediate acknowledgement if used by the child.

Peak: Step Back

In the peak phase, the thinking brain is offline. Behaviors may include physical aggression, property destruction, running away, or complete unresponsiveness. This is not the moment for teaching, reasoning, or prompting coping strategies. The focus is on safety, both physical and emotional, and following established protocols for ensuring a safe environment.

De-Escalation, Recovery, and the Debrief

As the child comes down from the peak, the de-escalation phase begins, which can look like disorientation, possibly blaming others, or sometimes trying to make up and move on immediately. Caregivers may want to debrief here as the incident is fresh, but that's the wrong timing.

In the recovery phase, the child slowly returns to baseline but may be subdued and able to complete only simple tasks. Here, the caregiver’s job is to quietly offer a bridge back: Welcome them back, reassure them, and communicate the belief that they can be successful.

The space to debrief belongs after the child is fully calm and re-engaged. Done well, the debrief phase can be collaborative and forward-looking: What set things off? What could be different next time? It is not a consequence conversation, and it shouldn't feel like one to the child. When it works, it can become the beginning of extending the next Calm phase.

The Question That Changes Everything

Understanding the escalation cycle reframes the whole task. The question shifts from "how do I stop this meltdown?" to "where are we in the cycle right now, and what does this moment call for me to do?"

That caregiver behavior shift from reactive to predictive is where adult leverage lives. Build the relationship and teach the skills during Calm. Read the early signals during Trigger and Agitation. Hold steady through Acceleration. Step back at Peak. Rebuild during Recovery. Debrief when the child is ready.

And occasionally, catch yourself mid-irritated-email and recognize: I'm in Agitation right now. Maybe this time I can take a pause and come back to send this later.

item.title: Why Winning an Argument Is Terrible for Your Sex Life
item.description:
Sex

Why Winning an Argument Is Terrible for Your Sex Life

The relational cost of needing to be right, and what it does to sexual desire.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • Winning an argument can boost your desire. The trouble is, it does the opposite to the person you just beat.
  • Conflict can trigger testosterone in men and cortisol in women, pulling one away from sexual desire.
  • Desire often depends less on resolution and more on emotional safety after disagreement.
  • Couples with great sex lives still argue. They just fight in a way that leaves both people still connected.

Mark, a 37-year-old engineer, came to therapy with a clear request: He wanted more sex with his wife, Sara. But within minutes, a related issue revealed itself. "When she challenges me, I know I'm right, and I want to win," he said, chest out, clearly relishing the thought. "And it feels good to win."

It does feel good to be right, doesn't it? Think back to the last argument you won. That satisfaction, that sense of being vindicated — it's real.

But that feeling may be quietly costing you your sex life.

Sara looked down as she listened to Mark and quietly said, "I just want to be heard. My opinion matters too, doesn't it?"

Just think about what happens after you "win" an argument. How does the rest of the evening go?
If you're honest, probably not great. The room can turn icy. Your partner can go quiet. You may want to reconnect and bask in your glory, but instead, you find them turning away.

Understanding what happens in the body during and after conflict can help to explain why "winning and losing" can change a couple's desire for sex later that night.

The Biology of Winning and Losing

Research into competition has found what is often called the "winner-loser effect." When people compete in sports, games, or social contests, winners tend to experience a rise in testosterone, while losers experience a drop. Because testosterone plays an important role in sexual desire in both men and women, these shifts can impact how much sex you (or your partner) want.

But intimate relationships are not simple competitions with clear winners and losers. Both partners are affected by conflict itself, and the experience is more physiologically complex than it first appears.

What changes first is not sexual desire directly; it is our body's readiness for closeness. And sexual desire, for most people, doesn't arise in a body braced for conflict. It arises in a body that feels safe, seen, and open. Conflict moves us in the opposite direction—toward self-protection, not self-disclosure. Toward winning, not wanting.

When the Competitive System Turns On

A study of 50 newlywed couples by Makhanova and colleagues (2018) found that conflict can affect men and women differently. Men who perceived their partner to be "oppositional" (disagreeing with them) showed increases in testosterone during conflict. They shift into a competitive, energized state, where they are more likely to argue harder, focus on being right, and feel justified in holding their position. The body is preparing for engagement and dominance—not softness, repair, or intimacy.

At the same time, the stress of conflict can activate cortisol, the body's primary stress hormone. Elevated cortisol is associated with emotional threat responses and can dampen sexual desire and receptivity, particularly in women.

After an argument, both partners may be physiologically dysregulated, just not in the same direction.

What Happens to the Couple

When two partners argue and one wins, one person may leave energised—even a little frisky. The other may feel emotionally shut down and no longer open to touch, closeness, or sexual connection.

The cruelest irony is that the person most likely to want physical connection after a conflict is the one who won it. And the person with whom they want reconnection is often the least available for it. This is not because they don't love each other, but because their nervous systems are no longer ready for sex.

The Need to Be Right May Be Costing You

I see a particular pattern in my sex therapy practice. One partner is what I call a high-need-to-win person. Intelligent, often right about things, and accustomed to resolving disagreements by pressing their case until the other person yields. They are not malicious. They often don't realize they're doing it.

These partners are frequently rewarded for competitiveness in other areas of life. At work, in sports, in debate, being dominant and "winning" can be adaptive and even admired.

But intimate relationships operate by different rules.

Research on testosterone and close relationships suggests that the same systems linked to competition and status can sometimes interfere with the responsiveness, emotional attunement, and mutuality that sustain desire over time.

Edelstein and colleagues (2014) found that men and women who report higher relationship satisfaction and commitment have lower levels of testosterone than those reporting lower satisfaction, which suggests that the competitive drive and the relational drive can work against each other. Lower testosterone may, in fact, be more beneficial for maintaining close relationships, even though we typically associate testosterone with sexual strength and drive.

The traits that help someone win in the outside world are not always the traits that help them stay emotionally and sexually connected at home.

What the "winner" may not realise is that every argument they win is a small withdrawal from the sexual and emotional bank account of their relationship, not because their partner is keeping score, but because their partner's body is consistently on the losing side.

Over time, repeatedly feeling unheard or overpowered in conflict may contribute to a general state of emotional withdrawal and reduced sexual desire. This is not about whether Sara liked sex overall. She did. It was her body turning sex off.

The partner who is always right wonders why the one they love doesn't seem to want them anymore.

What Actually Works

Change the goal. Instead of being right, the goal becomes being understood while also understanding your partner. It is a resolution where nobody leaves depleted or defeated.

The most sexually alive couples still argue. All couples do. But they tend to fight in a way that leaves both people feeling like they are still on the same team, even when they disagree.

Sexual desire is not only about attraction. It is about emotional safety, openness, and the sense that connection is still possible despite the fact that you are different people. In fact, attraction is because you are different people.

The Last Word for Sex

Managing arguments well is important. But if you want to invite your partner into sexual connection, it helps to understand what puts their nervous system into a state where arousal and desire can actually arise.

Research we are currently conducting (Zebroff & Thira) suggests that the strongest predictor of sexual initiation and satisfaction is not confidence, communication skill, or sexual technique, but whether partners accurately understand each other’s preferred initiation patterns.

Learning that pathway starts with understanding your own. Because sometimes, what stands between you and a satisfying sex life isn't performance, or technique, or confidence.

Sometimes it's just who won the last argument.

item.title: Why We Stay Longer Than We Should
item.description:
Relationships

Why We Stay Longer Than We Should

Delayed endings in relationships, work, family, and emotional attachment.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional disengagement often happens long before any visible separation occurs.
  • The sunk cost effect makes us stay in draining relationships due to past investment.
  • Loss aversion means the fear of loss often outweighs potential benefits of leaving.

Human relationships and commitments rarely end the moment they become painful. More often, they continue beyond the point of emotional fulfillment, long after something essential has changed. A romantic relationship may remain intact even after intimacy has weakened. A friendship may continue despite repeated disappointment or emotional imbalance. A workplace may still demand effort while no longer offering meaning, recognition, or psychological safety.

Family relationships may remain present through history or obligation while repeatedly leaving someone feeling criticised, dismissed, or emotionally depleted. In many of these situations, the external structure remains while the internal experience quietly shifts. What appears ongoing from the outside may already feel emotionally distant from within.

How Emotional Disengagement Precedes Visible Separation

Psychologically, this delayed ending is not unusual. Research suggests that emotional disengagement often begins well before any visible separation takes place. In close relationships, people may psychologically withdraw before they physically leave, moving through periods of internal doubt, emotional fatigue, or relational grief while remaining behaviourally committed (Joel et al., 2024). This creates a difficult emotional tension: recognising that something no longer feels healthy while still feeling unable, or unwilling, to let it go.

One explanation for this comes from the Investment Model of Commitment, which proposes that people remain committed not only because of satisfaction, but because of prior investment and perceived alternatives (Rusbult, 1980; Rusbult, 1983). Commitment is often built through accumulated time, emotional energy, shared memories, routines, sacrifices, loyalty, and imagined futures. The more someone has invested in a relationship, workplace, friendship, or family role, the harder it becomes psychologically to leave it. People are often attached not only to what something currently is, but to everything they have built around it over time.

Sunk Cost Effect in Emotional Life

This relates closely to the sunk cost effect, a concept in behavioural decision-making describing the tendency to continue investing in something because of what has already been invested, even when continuing may no longer be beneficial (Arkes & Blumer, 1985). Although commonly applied to financial decisions, it is equally relevant to emotional life. Time spent, effort given, emotional labour, sacrifice, and history can all become psychological reasons for staying. The internal reasoning may sound familiar: I’ve already given so much to this. I’ve stayed this long. Perhaps things will improve. Walking away now would make all of that meaningless. These beliefs can make disengagement emotionally difficult even when remaining feels draining.

Attachment processes further complicate these decisions. According to attachment theory, human beings are fundamentally organised around connection, security, and belonging (Bowlby, 1969). Over time, close relationships become emotionally regulating systems. Familiar people, environments, and routines can feel psychologically stabilising simply because they are known. This helps explain why people sometimes remain in relationships or environments that no longer feel nourishing. Familiarity can feel safer than uncertainty, even when familiarity is painful. Research on adult attachment consistently shows that emotional bonds influence how individuals respond to conflict, separation, and relational dissatisfaction, often making departure psychologically more difficult than expected (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2016).

Why Invalidating Relationships Persist Despite Emotional Pain

This is particularly visible in personal relationships marked by invalidation or emotional minimisation. People may remain connected to individuals who repeatedly dismiss their struggles, belittle their emotional experiences, or diminish their achievements. Emotional pain may be met with criticism instead of empathy. Success may be met with comparison instead of celebration. Over time, these dynamics can create exhaustion, self-doubt, and emotional strain. Yet such relationships often continue, not necessarily because they feel emotionally healthy, but because they are tied to history, identity, family roles, loyalty, or the hope that the dynamic may eventually change. Family systems theory highlights how long-standing relational patterns often persist despite causing distress precisely because they are deeply embedded within identity and relational structure (Kerr & Bowen, 1988).

Workplaces can operate in similar ways. Organisational psychology has shown that employees frequently remain in roles or institutions even when they feel chronically undervalued, emotionally exhausted, unsupported, or psychologically disconnected (Hom et al., 2017). Professional identity, financial dependency, loyalty to colleagues, institutional attachment, and fear of uncertainty often contribute to delayed departure. In some cases, people remain attached less to the current workplace itself and more to what it once represented, or what they hoped it would become.

Another important factor is loss aversion. Behavioural research consistently demonstrates that people experience losses more intensely than equivalent gains (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). This means the emotional pain associated with losing a relationship, role, community, or identity may feel stronger than the anticipated benefit of leaving it. Even when stepping away may create relief, freedom, or peace, the immediate psychological experience of loss can feel more powerful. As a result, remaining can sometimes feel emotionally easier than confronting the grief of departure.

Hope often sustains this process. Hope can be psychologically protective; it allows people to persist through difficulty, repair connections, and remain open to change. Yet hope can also delay endings. People may continue because they believe improvement is still possible, recognition may eventually come, the relationship may return to what it once was, or the next conversation may finally feel different. In this sense, people are often not only attached to the present reality, but to the future possibility of what something might still become.

Why Leaving Is Not Just a Rational Choice

Understanding why people stay longer than they feel they should requires moving beyond the assumption that leaving is a purely rational decision. Human commitment is rarely based on logic alone. It is shaped by attachment, investment, memory, hope, obligation, fear of loss, and identity. People stay because they care. They stay because they invested. They stay because they hoped. And often, they stay because letting go requires grieving not only what is ending now, but also what once mattered deeply, and what they once believed might still be possible.

Sometimes the most difficult endings are not sudden endings.

They are the ones that have been unfolding quietly for a long time while we are still trying to keep them alive.

item.title: Environmental Calm for the Autistic Nervous System
item.description:
Autism

Environmental Calm for the Autistic Nervous System

Why the wellness aesthetic that calms most people often fails autistic adults.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • The wellness aesthetic was developed for neurotypical nervous systems.
  • As many as 94 percent of autistic adults experience atypical sensory processing that affects daily function.
  • Calm is not a single visual look but a relationship between an environment and a nervous system.

The wellness aesthetic of the last decade has converged on a particular look. White or beige walls, mid-tone wood, neutral linen, scattered greenery, soft natural light. This visual vocabulary is so consistent across home design, spa branding, meditation apps, and therapy office Instagram accounts that it has become, in effect, the cultural shorthand for calm.

For many people, the aesthetic works quite well. The palette is restful, with warm tactile textures, and creates rooms that instantly calm the nervous system. However, for autistic adults, this same aesthetic often does almost nothing, and sometimes does the opposite. The space looks calm in photographs and feels unregulated in real life.

This design gap has actual consequences that extend well beyond interior design.

Source: Mateusz Pielech/Pexels

What sensory processing actually does

Sensory processing is the nervous system's ongoing work of receiving environmental input, organizing it, filtering it, and deciding what to attend to. For neurotypical people, a great deal of stimulus filtering happens automatically and below the level of conscious awareness. For autistic people, more energy is spent processing environmental stimuli.

As many as 94 percent of autistic adults experience atypical sensory processing significantly enough to affect daily function (Crane, Goddard, and Pring, 2009). The patterns vary individually, but several show up consistently across the research: lower thresholds for detecting environmental stimuli, slower habituation to ongoing sensory input, and greater fatigue from processing complex sensory environments over time (Bagatell, Chan, Syu, Lamarche, and Klinger, 2022).

A 2025 study in Scientific Reports found that the perceived aversiveness of someone's everyday auditory environment statistically mediates the relationship between autistic traits and overall quality of life (Poulsen et al., 2025). The sound of a place shapes livability. Other sensory modalities operate similarly. The visual texture, the acoustic reflection, the air quality, the artificial lighting, and the small ambient noises that neurotypical nervous systems filter out all register more intensely and linger longer for autistic adults.

This is not simply "heightened sensitivity" but is a structurally different relationship to the environment, one that asks more of the autistic nervous system at every moment than a neurotypical environment is typically designed to anticipate.

Why the wellness aesthetic often fails

The standard wellness palette was developed to soothe a neurotypical nervous system. Its design logic assumes the viewer's sensory filtering is already doing most of the work. Therefore, the space provides cues for a typical peaceful environment, and the brain responds accordingly.

For an autistic adult, the gaps in the design become the dominant experience. The bright white walls reflect harsh artificial light. The minimal furnishing leaves uncontained echoes. An exposed wood floor can amplify footfall and chair scrapes. Natural light shifts unpredictably across the day, requiring constant re-accommodation. In this case, the visual simplicity, intended as restful, can read as unfinished, leaving the nervous system without sufficient textural cues to settle and prompting it to seek completion of the open cognitive loop. In this way, the space can become antagonistic rather than restful.

What calm actually looks like

Autistic nervous systems find regulation in thoughtful containment rather than minimalism. The research and clinical literature on autism-supportive environmental design point toward several features that consistently support regulation (Black et al., 2022; Nagib and Williams, 2017).

Here are the environmental cues that signal regulation for autistic individuals:

  • Acoustic management through soft surfaces, such as rugs, curtains, upholstered furniture, and other textiles that absorb rather than reflect sound, is indicated. The goal is not stark silence, which can itself be dysregulating, but a controlled, predictable sound environment.
  • Predictable lighting. Warm, low-color-temperature artificial light. Dimmer controls. Lamps rather than overhead fixtures. Curtains or shades that allow control over the unpredictability of natural light.
  • Tactile density. Layered textures and materials that the eye can rest on without effort. This could include furnishings that signal comfort and provide ongoing low-level tactile reassurance.
  • Defined living zones. Clear boundaries between rooms or zones within rooms. This kind of spatial predictability reduces the cognitive load of orienting and re-orienting through the day.
  • Color depth. Saturated, deeper colors rather than the very pale neutrals of standard wellness design. Pale surfaces reflect more light and increase sensory input. Deeper colors absorb and contain. This runs counter to the dominant beige wellness aesthetic but closely aligns with what autistic adults often choose when given the freedom to do so.
  • Limited visual novelty. Spaces that change slowly. Rotating decor, frequent rearrangement, and high-stimulation visual variety can be exhausting to process. Familiarity reduces the cognitive cost of being at home.
Source: Matu Randall/Pexels

Of course, these are patterns, not rules. Sensory profiles vary substantially across the autistic population, and some autistic adults regulate better in spare, tonal, low-stimulus environments where layered textures would read as competing input rather than grounding. The research discussed here describes what supports regulation for many autistic adults, particularly those whose sensory profiles trend toward sensitivity and avoidance.

The deeper point

The goal is not to prescribe a single autism-friendly aesthetic. Autistic adults are individuals, and sensory profiles and tastes vary widely. What's important to realize is that calm is not a single visual look. Instead, it is a relationship between the environment and the nervous system, and a space that calms one kind of nervous system may quietly drain another.

If you are autistic or have a highly sensitive nervous system and you have spent years wondering why the homes you are supposed to find restful leave you feeling uncomfortable, ask yourself what your nervous system actually needs to feel regulated and note that it may not be in step with design conventions of "calm."

item.title: Guilt and Shame Don't Always Mean You Made a Bad Choice
item.description:
Boundaries

Guilt and Shame Don't Always Mean You Made a Bad Choice

Learn to trust your thoughtful decisions.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • Just because you've been given a role doesn't mean that role is healthy, fair, or what defines you.
  • Feeling guilt or shame after making a healthy decision may mean that you need stronger boundaries.
  • Have compassion for yourself when you set a boundary.

You are not and never will be perfect. You can't make everyone happy all of the time. These truths may be uncomfortable, but hopefully, also freeing.

Navigating Expectations

Humans live in layers of systems (e.g., family, friends, colleagues, local community, country), and being part of those systems comes with expectations. Those expectations are normal and part of what helps us work together in teams. For example, expecting each member of the team to contribute or to follow certain rules, like driving on the correct side of the road for their current location.

Source: Javier Allegue Barros / Unsplash

Nevertheless, it can be hard to know how to create healthy boundaries around expectations that others have placed on you that are outside of the functional, agreed-upon norms and/or are not healthy for you. People in your life, often family, friends, or colleagues, may place expectations on you that do not align with how you feel, what you believe, or what feels healthiest for you.

For instance, as the eldest daughter, you may have been expected to care for your younger siblings, and now, as an adult, you're expected to take on the responsibility of caring for your aging parents. The same expectations may not have been placed on your younger siblings or your brothers.

Those in the sandwich generation, who are providing care for aging parents and their own young children, may be subjected to excessive or unrealistic expectations, but others also endure this. For example, at work, you may experience moral injury when you are told you need to add a new step to your current process but are not given the resources or time to do so.

You are likely a kind person who wants to contribute to your family and support your loved ones, but you may need to place limits on how much mental, emotional, and physical energy you can give in one area of your life, knowing that there are others who count on you, including yourself.

Guilt and Shame

When you set limits on the time and energy you give to others, they will react. The response may include acceptance and understanding or resistance and emotional pleas. They may intentionally or unintentionally make you feel guilty (i.e., like you've done something bad) and/or ashamed (i.e., like you are bad). As you navigate these feelings of guilt or shame, it's important to thoughtfully find healthy ways to check in with yourself, self-soothe, and coach yourself.

Check In With Yourself

It can be hard to set and stick to healthy boundaries, especially if those around you are making you feel like you are not living up to their expectations. When you experience a negative emotion after setting a health boundary, ask yourself/reflect on the following:

  • What are all the healthy reasons I made this decision?
  • What would be the emotional, mental, and physical costs of my going back on the healthy decision I made for myself?
  • What would help me trust myself more in these moments?
  • What would I say to someone I care about if they were in my position?

Self-soothe

Take time to engage in calming and soothing activities when you start to feel these emotions. This can include any healthy activity that helps you feel calmer and grounded where you are in the moment.

This might include:

  • Taking 20 slow, deep breaths
  • Noticing, without judging, 5 things you see, 4 things you can touch, 3 things you hear, 2 things you smell, and 1 thing you taste
  • Closing your eyes and imagining yourself walking through your favorite space (e.g., on the beach, in the woods, in your bedroom), and noticing in detail what you imagine seeing, touching, hearing, smelling, and tasting

Coach Yourself

Setting boundaries can feel uncomfortable, especially when doing so is new. It's important to be an ally to yourself in these moments and to remain open to feedback while also recognizing the unhelpful thoughts and beliefs keeping you stuck in old patterns.

Engage in some meta-cognition (i.e., think about your thoughts) and reflect on the following:

  • What's leading you to doubt yourself?
  • How do you think you are supposed to act and feel?
  • What is expected of you, and what negative emotions come along with not living up to those expectations?
  • What unhelpful thoughts are keeping you stuck in feelings of guilt and shame? How are those thoughts unrealistic and unfair to you?
  • What makes it important to stick to this healthy change even though it's uncomfortable?

Overall, it's important to reassure yourself that you are allowed to make decisions that include you as a priority. You cannot be everything for everyone. It's OK if others are frustrated with you at times. If you are looking for an internal compass to help guide your decisions, look to your values. Find balance in living your values and finding ways to include yourself and your needs in the decisions you make around supporting others. It's not selfish to remember that you matter too and to set healthy boundaries.

item.title: When the World Feels Too Much: Grieving the Loss of Certainty
item.description:
Anxiety

When the World Feels Too Much: Grieving the Loss of Certainty

Many people may be mourning a predictable future without realizing it.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional distress about the future may sometimes reflect grief rather than fear alone.
  • People can mourn lost expectations, imagined futures, and assumptions about how life was supposed to unfold.
  • Resilience grows through adaptability, strong relationships, and self-trust, not certainty.

Many people describe feeling anxious, overwhelmed, distracted, or emotionally exhausted these days. They worry about the future and their careers. They worry about their children. They worry about technology, politics, economics, climate change, and the pace of social change.

Yet beneath many of these concerns, there may be another emotional experience that often goes unnamed: Grief. Not grief for a person. Not grief for a relationship. But grief for certainty itself.

The Future Once Felt More Predictable

Every generation has faced uncertainty. Life has never come with guarantees.

Yet many people today are navigating a unique combination of rapid technological change, political polarization, economic instability, environmental concerns, and shifting social norms. As a result, assumptions that once felt relatively stable may feel less reliable than they once did.

Many people grew up believing that hard work would lead to security, that institutions would provide stability, and that the future would be easier to imagine than it is now. Whether these beliefs were accurate is less important than the role they played. They helped people make sense of their lives and plan for what came next.

When those assumptions begin to feel less dependable, people can experience a profound sense of disorientation.

When Anxiety Masks Loss

Most people recognize grief when they lose someone they love. But grief is not limited to death. People grieve lost opportunities, lost identities, lost dreams, and lost versions of themselves. They can also grieve lost expectations.

Sometimes what appears to be anxiety is actually a response to the disappearance of a future that once felt imaginable. A person may have expected a certain career path, financial stability, social environment, or vision of the world. When those expectations become uncertain, the emotional response can resemble grief as much as fear.

The challenge is that society rarely teaches us to recognize this kind of loss. Instead, people often assume they are simply anxious, unmotivated, or struggling to cope.

Why Uncertainty Feels So Uncomfortable

Human beings naturally seek patterns. We create routines. We build traditions, and we develop beliefs about how the world works. These structures help us feel safe because they make life more predictable.

When uncertainty increases, many people respond by searching for stronger forms of control. They may become preoccupied with planning, consume endless information, or look for simple answers to complex problems.

These responses are understandable. They often represent attempts to restore a sense of safety in an environment that feels increasingly difficult to predict.

The problem is that certainty and safety are not always the same thing. Sometimes the pursuit of certainty creates more distress than uncertainty itself.

Building Stability Without Guarantees

Psychological well-being does not require knowing exactly what will happen next. It requires developing the capacity to move forward despite not knowing.

This is not resignation or passivity. It is adaptation.

From a systemic perspective, resilience emerges not from controlling every outcome but from strengthening the relationships, values, and communities that help us navigate change.

While we cannot eliminate uncertainty, we can cultivate resources that make uncertainty easier to tolerate. We can pursue meaningful relationships, seek out purpose, increase flexibility, create connection, and build self-trust. These forms of stability often prove more durable than the predictions we make about the future.

A Different Kind of Security

Perhaps one of the hidden challenges of modern life is learning to let go of the belief that security comes from certainty. Perhaps security comes from something deeper.

  • The confidence that we can adapt when circumstances change.
  • The knowledge that we can seek support when life becomes difficult.
  • The trust that uncertainty does not automatically mean danger.

The future has always contained unanswered questions. What may be different today is how aware we are of them.

Recognizing the grief that can accompany uncertainty does not remove it. But it may help us approach ourselves with greater compassion as we learn to live, plan, and hope in a world that offers fewer guarantees than we once imagined.
